questions.topic: Unit 2 (Livestock Production): Livestock: Care, Management and Diseases
questions.sub_topic: Housing systems and their features
questions.question:
Match List-I (Housing system) with List-II (Feature).

List-I
(A) Deep litter
(B) Battery cage
(C) Free range
(D) Loose housing

List-II
(I) Cattle move freely in an open paddock with shelter on one side
(II) Birds live on a thick floor layer of husk or sawdust
(III) Birds roam outdoors by day and shelter at night
(IV) Birds are kept in tiers of wire cages
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
Why: In deep litter, birds live on a thick bed of husk or sawdust (II). In battery cages they are kept in tiers of wire cages (IV). Free-range birds roam outdoors (III). In loose housing, cattle move freely in a paddock with a shelter (I).
Why not the others: Option (B) swaps deep litter and battery cage. Option (C) swaps free range and loose housing. Option (D) swaps battery cage and free range.
Key point: Deep litter and cages are for poultry; loose housing is for cattle.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Biochemistry
questions.sub_topic: Levels of protein structure in order
questions.question:
Arrange the levels of protein structure from the simplest to the most complex.
(A) Tertiary structure
(B) Primary structure
(C) Quaternary structure
(D) Secondary structure
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B), (D), (A), (C)
Why: The primary structure (B) is the sequence of amino acids. The secondary structure (D) is local folding into helices and sheets. The tertiary structure (A) is the three-dimensional folding of one chain. The quaternary structure (C) is the assembly of two or more chains.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts tertiary before secondary. Option (C) starts with secondary. Option (D) puts quaternary before tertiary.
Key point: Primary → secondary → tertiary → quaternary.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Microbiology
questions.sub_topic: Why wide C:N residues lock up nitrogen
questions.question: Why does adding wheat straw, which has a wide C:N ratio, often cause a temporary nitrogen shortage for the next crop?
options: A) Because microbes decomposing the straw take up soil nitrogen for their own growth
B) Because straw releases ammonia gas that escapes from the soil into the air
C) Because straw contains a chemical that kills the nitrogen-fixing bacteria
D) Because straw raises soil pH so much that all the nitrate is lost
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Because microbes decomposing the straw take up soil nitrogen for their own growth
Why: Microbes need nitrogen to build their cells while they break down carbon-rich straw. They take it from the soil, so it is not available to the crop until they die and release it (immobilisation).
Why not the others:
(B) Straw is poor in nitrogen; it does not release much ammonia.
(C) Straw does not contain such a chemical.
(D) Straw does not sharply raise soil pH.
Key point: Wide C:N residues cause temporary nitrogen immobilisation.

questions.topic: Unit 4 (Horticulture): Horticulture: Importance, Orchards, Gardens and Propagation
questions.sub_topic: Why perennials go on one side of a kitchen garden
questions.question: Why are perennial plants such as drumstick, papaya and curry leaf grown along one side of a kitchen garden?
options: A) So that they do not shade the seasonal vegetable beds
B) Because perennials need more water than any vegetable
C) So that the garden looks symmetrical from the road
D) Because perennials repel all insect pests from vegetables
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) So that they do not shade the seasonal vegetable beds
Why: Perennials stay for years and grow tall. On one side (usually the north) they do not shade the seasonal beds and do not get in the way of digging.
Why not the others:
(B) Water need is not the reason.
(C) Appearance is not the reason.
(D) They do not repel all pests.
Key point: Plan the kitchen garden so tall perennials do not shade the beds.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Crop Production: Introduction and Modern Agriculture
questions.sub_topic: What jeevamrit is in natural farming
questions.question: In natural farming, 'jeevamrit' is:
options: A) a synthetic growth regulator sprayed on the leaves
B) a low-cost drip irrigation kit for small farms
C) a drought-hardy variety of millet for dry areas
D) a fermented mix of dung, urine, jaggery and pulse flour
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) a fermented mix of dung, urine, jaggery and pulse flour
Why: Jeevamrit is a fermented preparation made from cow dung, cow urine, jaggery, pulse flour and a little soil. It is applied to boost soil microbial activity.
Why not the others:
(A) Natural farming avoids synthetic inputs.
(B) It is not an irrigation system.
(C) It is not a crop variety.
Key point: Jeevamrit feeds soil microbes in natural farming.

questions.topic: Unit 4 (Horticulture): Cultivation of Fruits, Vegetables and Flowers
questions.sub_topic: Crop to which Alphonso belongs
questions.question: 'Alphonso' is a famous variety of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) mango
Why: Alphonso is a premium mango variety of Maharashtra's Konkan coast.
Why not the others: Guava varieties include Allahabad Safeda, banana varieties include Grand Naine, and grape varieties include Thompson Seedless.
Key point: Alphonso is mango.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Microbiology
questions.sub_topic: A eukaryotic microorganism
questions.question: Which of the following microorganisms is a eukaryote?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Yeast
Why: Yeast is a fungus; its cells have a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
Why not the others: (A) *Rhizobium* is a bacterium, (B) *Nostoc* is a cyanobacterium and (C) *Streptomyces* is an actinomycete. All three are prokaryotes.
Key point: Fungi, algae (other than blue-green) and protozoa are eukaryotes; bacteria and actinomycetes are prokaryotes.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Crop Production: Introduction and Modern Agriculture
questions.sub_topic: Crop that is not grown for fibre
questions.question: From the point of view of crop classification, which one of the following does NOT belong with the fibre crops?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Castor
Why: Castor is a non-edible oilseed crop.
Why not the others: (B) jute, (C) cotton and (D) mesta are fibre crops.
Key point: Fibre crops: cotton, jute, mesta and sunn hemp.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Field Crops: Cultivation, Protection and Post-harvest
questions.sub_topic: Crop diseases and their pathogens
questions.question:
Match List-I (Disease) with List-II (Pathogen).

List-I
(A) Blast of rice
(B) Red rot of sugarcane
(C) Tikka of groundnut
(D) Wilt of pigeon pea

List-II
(I) *Fusarium udum*
(II) *Cercospora* species
(III) *Colletotrichum falcatum*
(IV) *Magnaporthe oryzae* (*Pyricularia oryzae*)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: Rice blast is caused by *Magnaporthe oryzae* (IV). Red rot of sugarcane is caused by *Colletotrichum falcatum* (III). Tikka leaf spot of groundnut is caused by *Cercospora* (II). Pigeon pea wilt is caused by *Fusarium udum* (I).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps blast and red rot. Option (B) swaps red rot and tikka. Option (C) swaps tikka and wilt.
Key point: All four are fungal diseases; know the genus behind each.

questions.topic: Unit 2 (Livestock Production): Artificial Insemination and Livestock Products
questions.sub_topic: Product made by acid coagulation of hot milk
questions.question: Which milk product is made by curdling hot milk with an acid such as citric acid and pressing the curd?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Paneer
Why: Paneer is made by acid coagulation of hot milk, then draining and pressing the curd.
Why not the others:
(A) Khoa is made by evaporating milk.
(C) Ghee is clarified butterfat.
(D) Dahi is made by bacterial fermentation.
Key point: Paneer — acid; dahi — bacteria; khoa — evaporation.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Seed Science
questions.sub_topic: Seed dormancy — which statement is wrong
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about seed dormancy:
(A) A hard, impermeable seed coat is a common cause of dormancy in legumes.
(B) Scarification helps to break dormancy caused by the seed coat.
(C) Dormant seeds are dead and can never germinate later.
(D) Gibberellic acid can break dormancy in some seeds.
Which of the statements given above is NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C) only
Why: (C) is false: dormant seeds are alive. They simply do not germinate until the cause of dormancy is removed. (A), (B) and (D) are true.
Why not the others: Statements (A), (B) and (D) are all correct.
Key point: Dormancy is a resting state of a living seed.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Irrigation and Drainage
questions.sub_topic: Methods of irrigation — which are wrong
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Border strip irrigation suits close-growing crops such as wheat.
(B) Furrow irrigation suits row crops such as maize and sugarcane.
(C) Wild flooding has the highest application efficiency of all methods.
(D) Sprinkler irrigation works best in very windy areas.
Which of the statements given above are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (C) and (D) only
Why: (A) and (B) are true. (C) is false: wild flooding wastes much water and has low efficiency. (D) is false: strong wind distorts the spray of sprinklers, so they work poorly in windy areas.
Why not the others: Option (A) calls the true statement (A) wrong. Option (B) calls the true statement (B) wrong. Option (C) misses statement (C).
Key point: Flooding is wasteful; sprinklers dislike wind.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Biochemistry
questions.sub_topic: Chemical nature of most enzymes
questions.question: Most enzymes are ________ in chemical nature.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) proteins
Why: Almost all enzymes are proteins that speed up reactions without being used up. A few RNA molecules (ribozymes) also act as catalysts.
Why not the others: (A) lipids, (B) carbohydrates and (C) nucleotides are not the usual chemical basis of enzymes.
Key point: Enzymes are biological catalysts, mostly proteins.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Soil, Soil Fertility, Fertilizers and Manures
questions.sub_topic: Soil types of India and their features
questions.question:
Match List-I (Soil) with List-II (Feature).

List-I
(A) Alluvial soil
(B) Black soil
(C) Red soil
(D) Laterite soil

List-II
(I) Formed by intense leaching under heavy rainfall; rich in iron and aluminium
(II) Swells when wet and cracks when dry; well suited to cotton
(III) Deposited by rivers; covers the Indo-Gangetic plains
(IV) Colour from iron oxides; usually poor in nitrogen and phosphorus
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(II), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)
Why: Alluvial soils are river deposits of the Indo-Gangetic plains (III). Black soils swell and crack and suit cotton (II). Red soils owe their colour to iron oxides and are poor in N and P (IV). Laterite soils form by heavy leaching and are rich in iron and aluminium (I).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps black and red soils. Option (B) swaps alluvial and black soils. Option (D) swaps red and laterite soils.
Key point: River plains — alluvial; cotton — black; iron colour — red; leached — laterite.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Seed Science
questions.sub_topic: Products of double fertilisation
questions.question: In flowering plants, double fertilisation produces:
options: A) two separate zygotes, both of them diploid, in each ovule
B) a diploid zygote and a triploid primary endosperm nucleus
C) a haploid zygote and a diploid endosperm nucleus
D) a triploid zygote and a diploid endosperm nucleus
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) a diploid zygote and a triploid primary endosperm nucleus
Why: One male gamete fuses with the egg to form the diploid zygote. The other fuses with the two polar nuclei to form the triploid primary endosperm nucleus.
Why not the others:
(A) Only one zygote is formed.
(C) The zygote is diploid and the endosperm triploid.
(D) This reverses the ploidy levels.
Key point: Syngamy + triple fusion = double fertilisation.

questions.topic: Unit 2 (Livestock Production): Livestock: Care, Management and Diseases
questions.sub_topic: Type of agent causing foot-and-mouth disease
questions.question: Foot-and-mouth disease, which causes blisters in the mouth and on the feet of cattle, is caused by a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) virus
Why: FMD is caused by an aphthovirus. It spreads fast, and vaccination is the main means of control.
Why not the others: The agent is a virus, not (A) a bacterium, (B) a protozoan or (D) a fungus.
Key point: FMD is viral; vaccinate the herd regularly.

questions.topic: Unit 4 (Horticulture): Cultivation of Fruits, Vegetables and Flowers
questions.sub_topic: Flowers and their planting material
questions.question:
Match List-I (Flower crop) with List-II (Common planting material).

List-I
(A) Gladiolus
(B) Rose
(C) Canna
(D) Chrysanthemum

List-II
(I) Rhizomes
(II) Corms
(III) Terminal cuttings and suckers
(IV) T-budding on a rootstock
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: Gladiolus is grown from corms (II). Roses are commonly T-budded on a rootstock (IV). Canna is grown from rhizomes (I). Chrysanthemum is raised from terminal cuttings and suckers (III).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps gladiolus and canna. Option (B) swaps rose and chrysanthemum. Option (D) swaps gladiolus and rose.
Key point: Gladiolus — corms; canna — rhizomes; rose — budding; chrysanthemum — cuttings.

questions.topic: Unit 2 (Livestock Production): Artificial Insemination and Livestock Products
questions.sub_topic: Milk with higher fat content
questions.question: Compared with cow milk, buffalo milk has a noticeably higher content of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) fat
Why: Buffalo milk has about 6–8% fat, against about 3.5–4.5% in cow milk, which makes it richer and better for ghee.
Why not the others:
(B) Buffalo milk has less water because it has more solids.
(C) Lactose is about the same in both.
(D) Milk of both is poor in iron.
Key point: Buffalo milk is richer in fat.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Soil, Soil Fertility, Fertilizers and Manures
questions.sub_topic: Nutrient deficiency shown by purple leaves
questions.question: Purple colouring of the leaves, especially in young maize plants, is a typical sign of a deficiency of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) phosphorus
Why: Phosphorus deficiency leads to the build-up of anthocyanin pigments, so leaves turn purple, especially in cool weather.
Why not the others:
(B) Nitrogen deficiency causes yellowing of older leaves.
(C) Potassium deficiency scorches leaf margins.
(D) Sulphur deficiency yellows young leaves.
Key point: Purple — phosphorus; yellow older leaves — nitrogen; scorched edges — potassium.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Genetics and Plant Breeding
questions.sub_topic: Crop that is not cross-pollinated
questions.question: Which of the following crops is NOT cross-pollinated?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Wheat
Why: Wheat is a self-pollinated crop: its flowers usually pollinate themselves before they open.
Why not the others: (B) maize, (C) pearl millet and (D) sunflower are cross-pollinated crops.
Key point: Wheat, rice, gram and groundnut are self-pollinated; maize and bajra are cross-pollinated.

questions.topic: Unit 2 (Livestock Production): Fisheries
questions.sub_topic: Characteristics of fish — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Fish breathe mainly through gills.
(B) Fish are cold-blooded; their body temperature changes with the water.
(C) All fish are covered with scales.
(D) Fins help fish to move and keep their balance.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: (A), (B) and (D) are true. (C) is false: some fish, such as many catfishes, have no scales.
Why not the others: Options (A), (C) and (D) all include the false statement (C).
Key point: Gills, fins and cold blood mark fish; scales are common but not universal.

questions.topic: Unit 4 (Horticulture): Horticulture: Importance, Orchards, Gardens and Propagation
questions.sub_topic: Woody plant with many stems from the base
questions.question: A woody plant with several stems arising from near the ground and no single main trunk is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) a shrub
Why: Shrubs are woody plants with several stems from the base, such as hibiscus.
Why not the others:
(A) A tree has a single main trunk.
(B) A climber needs support to grow upward.
(C) An annual is defined by life span, not form.
Key point: Shrubs are bushy and woody; trees have one trunk.

questions.topic: Unit 2 (Livestock Production): Livestock: Care, Management and Diseases
questions.sub_topic: Not a sign of a sick animal
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a sign that a farm animal is sick?
options: A) It stops eating and stays apart from the herd.
B) Its coat looks rough and dull.
C) It has a high temperature and dull eyes.
D) It has bright eyes and a cool, moist muzzle.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) It has bright eyes and a cool, moist muzzle.
Why: Bright eyes and a moist muzzle are signs of a healthy animal.
Why not the others: (A) loss of appetite and isolation, (B) a rough coat and (C) fever with dull eyes all indicate sickness.
Key point: A moist muzzle and bright eyes mean health; a dry muzzle and dull eyes mean trouble.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Weed Control
questions.sub_topic: Weed characteristics — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about weeds:
(A) Weeds often produce very large numbers of seeds.
(B) Many weed seeds stay dormant but alive in the soil for years.
(C) Weeds compete with crops for light, water and nutrients.
(D) Some weeds act as alternate hosts for crop pests and diseases.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B), (C) and (D)
Why: All four are true. Prolific seeding and long seed dormancy make weeds persistent, they compete for resources, and many shelter pests and pathogens.
Why not the others: Options (A), (B) and (D) each leave out at least one true statement.
Key point: Weeds harm crops directly by competition and indirectly by hosting pests.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Crop Production: Introduction and Modern Agriculture
questions.sub_topic: Crop first boosted by the Green Revolution
questions.question: The Green Revolution of the late 1960s first raised the production of which crop most sharply in India?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Wheat
Why: Semi-dwarf, fertilizer-responsive wheat varieties brought the steepest early rise; rice followed.
Why not the others: (A) pulses, (B) cotton and (D) oilseeds gained much less at the time.
Key point: The Green Revolution was first a wheat revolution.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Field Crops: Cultivation, Protection and Post-harvest
questions.sub_topic: Safe moisture for storing wheat grain
questions.question: For safe storage, wheat grain should be dried to a moisture content of about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 10–12 percent
Why: At about 10–12% moisture, moulds and insects cannot multiply easily in stored wheat.
Why not the others:
(A) and (B) are far too moist; the grain will heat and spoil.
(D) Drying so far is unnecessary and costly, and it cracks the grain.
Key point: Dry grain stores well; aim for about 10–12% moisture.

questions.topic: Unit 4 (Horticulture): Horticulture: Importance, Orchards, Gardens and Propagation
questions.sub_topic: Training and pruning — which statement is wrong
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Training gives a young tree a desired shape and a strong framework.
(B) In the open-centre system, the main stem is allowed to grow upward unchecked.
(C) Pruning removes dead, diseased and crowded shoots.
(D) Grapevines are pruned every year.
Which of the statements given above is NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B) only
Why: (B) is false: in the open-centre system the main stem is headed back so that the tree has an open, vase-shaped centre. Unchecked growth of the main stem describes the central leader system. (A), (C) and (D) are true.
Why not the others: Statements (A), (C) and (D) are all correct.
Key point: Open centre = vase shape; central leader = one dominant trunk.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Agrometeorology
questions.sub_topic: Term for long-term average weather
questions.question: The average condition of the atmosphere at a place over a long period, usually about 30 years, is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) climate
Why: Climate is the long-term average of weather; weather is the state of the atmosphere at a given time.
Why not the others:
(A) Weather is short-term.
(B) A season is one part of a year.
(D) A forecast predicts future weather.
Key point: Weather is today; climate is the long-term average.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Agrometeorology
questions.sub_topic: Weather instruments and what they record
questions.question:
Match List-I (Instrument) with List-II (What it records).

List-I
(A) Anemometer
(B) Wind vane
(C) Campbell–Stokes recorder
(D) Rain gauge

List-II
(I) Rainfall
(II) Duration of bright sunshine
(III) Wind speed
(IV) Wind direction
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: The anemometer records wind speed (III). The wind vane shows wind direction (IV). The Campbell–Stokes recorder burns a trace on a card to record hours of bright sunshine (II). The rain gauge measures rainfall (I).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps the anemometer and wind vane. Option (C) swaps the sunshine recorder and rain gauge. Option (D) swaps the wind vane and sunshine recorder.
Key point: Speed — anemometer; direction — vane; sunshine — Campbell–Stokes.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Soil, Soil Fertility, Fertilizers and Manures
questions.sub_topic: Order of steps in taking a soil sample
questions.question:
Arrange the steps of taking a soil sample for testing in the correct order.
(A) Air-dry, sieve and label the sample
(B) Mix the slices and reduce the sample by quartering
(C) Make a V-shaped cut to plough depth and take a slice from its side
(D) Scrape away the surface litter at the sampling spot
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (D), (C), (B), (A)
Why: First the surface litter is scraped away (D). Then a V-shaped cut is made and a slice taken (C). Slices from many spots are mixed and reduced by quartering (B). Finally the sample is air-dried, sieved and labelled (A).
Why not the others: Option (A) cuts before clearing the spot. Option (B) dries before mixing. Option (C) mixes before collecting.
Key point: Clear → cut → mix and quarter → dry and label.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Biochemistry
questions.sub_topic: Carbohydrates and their roles
questions.question:
Match List-I (Carbohydrate) with List-II (Description).

List-I
(A) Ribose
(B) Starch
(C) Glycogen
(D) Cellulose

List-II
(I) Storage polysaccharide of plants
(II) Pentose sugar found in RNA
(III) Structural polysaccharide of the plant cell wall
(IV) Storage polysaccharide of animals
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)
Why: Ribose is the pentose sugar of RNA (II). Starch is the storage polysaccharide of plants (I). Glycogen is the storage polysaccharide of animals (IV). Cellulose builds the plant cell wall (III).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps ribose and starch. Option (B) swaps glycogen and cellulose. Option (C) swaps starch and glycogen.
Key point: Starch stores food in plants, glycogen in animals; cellulose builds walls.

questions.topic: Unit 4 (Horticulture): Fruit and Vegetable Preservation
questions.sub_topic: Order of steps in making potato chips
questions.question:
Arrange the steps of making potato chips in the correct order.
(A) Frying
(B) Slicing
(C) Blanching
(D) Washing and peeling
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (D), (B), (C), (A)
Why: Potatoes are first washed and peeled (D) and then sliced thin (B). The slices are blanched (C) to inactivate enzymes and remove surface starch, and then fried (A).
Why not the others: Option (B) slices before washing. Option (C) blanches before slicing. Option (D) fries before blanching.
Key point: Wash/peel → slice → blanch → fry → pack.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Genetics and Plant Breeding
questions.sub_topic: Polygenic inheritance — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Quantitative traits such as yield and plant height show continuous variation.
(B) Polygenic traits are controlled by many genes, each with a small effect.
(C) Discontinuous variation gives distinct classes, such as tall and dwarf pea plants.
(D) The environment has no effect on quantitative traits.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) are true. (D) is false: quantitative traits are strongly influenced by the environment, such as soil fertility and water.
Why not the others: Options (B) and (C) include the false statement (D). Option (D) leaves out the true statement (C).
Key point: Polygenic traits vary continuously and respond to the environment.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Irrigation and Drainage
questions.sub_topic: Order of irrigation stages of wheat
questions.question:
Arrange the following irrigation stages of wheat in the order in which they occur in the crop.
(A) Tillering
(B) Flowering
(C) Crown root initiation
(D) Jointing
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C), (A), (D), (B)
Why: Crown root initiation (C) comes at about 20–25 days. Tillering (A) follows at about 40–45 days. Jointing (D) comes at about 60–65 days. Flowering (B) comes at about 80–85 days.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts tillering before CRI. Option (B) puts jointing before tillering. Option (D) puts flowering before jointing.
Key point: CRI → tillering → jointing → flowering → milk → dough.

questions.topic: Unit 4 (Horticulture): Fruit and Vegetable Preservation
questions.sub_topic: Preservative used in tomato ketchup
questions.question: Which chemical preservative is commonly used in tomato ketchup?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Sodium benzoate
Why: Sodium benzoate is the usual preservative for ketchup and other coloured products, because it does not bleach colour.
Why not the others:
(A) Potassium nitrate is a fertilizer and curing salt, not used in ketchup.
(B) Copper sulphate is a fungicide.
(D) Calcium carbide is a banned ripening agent.
Key point: Coloured products such as ketchup use sodium benzoate.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Soil, Soil Fertility, Fertilizers and Manures
questions.sub_topic: Amendment for sodic soils
questions.question: Which amendment is commonly used to reclaim sodic (alkali) soils?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Gypsum
Why: Gypsum (calcium sulphate) supplies calcium, which replaces sodium on the soil clay. The sodium is then washed out with water.
Why not the others:
(A) Lime is used to correct acid soils.
(C) Urea and (D) MOP are fertilizers, not amendments.
Key point: Acid soil — lime; sodic soil — gypsum.

questions.topic: Unit 4 (Horticulture): Cultivation of Fruits, Vegetables and Flowers
questions.sub_topic: Cause of black tip in mango
questions.question: 'Black tip' of mango, in which the tip of the fruit turns black and hard, is caused mainly by:
options: A) a fungal attack during storage
B) boron deficiency in sandy soils
C) attack by the mango hopper
D) fumes from nearby brick kilns
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) fumes from nearby brick kilns
Why: Gases such as sulphur dioxide from brick kilns injure the young fruit and cause black tip. Spraying borax helps to reduce it.
Why not the others:
(A) It is not a storage fungus.
(B) Boron sprays help reduce black tip, but boron deficiency is not its main cause.
(C) The hopper damages the flowers, not the fruit tip.
Key point: Keep brick kilns away from mango orchards.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Genetics and Plant Breeding
questions.sub_topic: Number of gametes from a trihybrid
questions.question: How many genetically different gametes can a plant of genotype AaBbCc produce, if the three genes assort independently?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 8
Why: Step 1: each heterozygous gene gives 2 kinds of gametes.
Step 2: with n independent heterozygous genes, the number of gamete types is 2ⁿ.
Step 3: n = 3, so 2³ = 8 (ABC, ABc, AbC, Abc, aBC, aBc, abC, abc).
Why not the others:
(A) 3 is just the number of genes.
(B) 4 is the answer for two heterozygous genes.
(C) 6 is 2 × 3, which is not how gametes combine.
Key point: Gamete types = 2ⁿ, where n is the number of heterozygous gene pairs.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Agrometeorology
questions.sub_topic: Basis of Köppen's climate classification
questions.question: Köppen's classification of climates is based mainly on:
options: A) temperature and precipitation, as reflected in natural vegetation
B) wind direction and air pressure in the different seasons of the year
C) soil type, drainage and the depth of the water table below ground
D) latitude and altitude alone, without any weather records
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) temperature and precipitation, as reflected in natural vegetation
Why: Köppen used monthly and annual temperature and precipitation, linked to the types of natural vegetation they support.
Why not the others:
(B) Wind and pressure are not his main criteria.
(C) Soil and water table are not used.
(D) Latitude and altitude alone do not define his climate classes.
Key point: Köppen's classes rest on temperature, rainfall and vegetation.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Microbiology
questions.sub_topic: Microbes that set milk into curd
questions.question: Which microorganisms turn milk into curd?
options: B) Lactic acid bacteria such as *Lactobacillus*
C) Blue-green algae such as *Anabaena* and *Nostoc*
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Lactic acid bacteria such as *Lactobacillus*
Why: *Lactobacillus* and related bacteria ferment lactose into lactic acid, which curdles the milk protein.
Why not the others:
(A) Yeasts produce alcohol and carbon dioxide.
(C) Blue-green algae are photosynthetic.
(D) Actinomycetes are soil decomposers.
Key point: Curd is made by lactic acid bacteria.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Field Crops: Cultivation, Protection and Post-harvest
questions.sub_topic: Crop attacked by pink bollworm
questions.question: The pink bollworm is a major pest of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) cotton
Why: Pink bollworm larvae bore into cotton bolls and damage the seed and lint.
Why not the others: (A) groundnut, (C) sugarcane and (D) mustard have other key pests, such as leaf miner, early shoot borer and aphid.
Key point: Bollworms are pests of cotton.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Weed Control
questions.sub_topic: Biological agent against Parthenium
questions.question: Which insect is used for the biological control of *Parthenium hysterophorus* (carrot grass)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) *Zygogramma bicolorata*
Why: The Mexican beetle *Zygogramma bicolorata* feeds on Parthenium leaves.
Why not the others:
(B) *Neochetina* weevils control water hyacinth.
(C) *Cactoblastis* controls prickly pear.
(D) *Trichogramma* is an egg parasitoid of insect pests, not a weed-feeder.
Key point: Parthenium — *Zygogramma*; water hyacinth — *Neochetina*; prickly pear — *Cactoblastis*.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Genetics and Plant Breeding
questions.sub_topic: Crops suited to pure-line selection
questions.question: Pure-line selection, based on the work of W.L. Johannsen, is a breeding method suited mainly to:
options: A) cross-pollinated crops such as maize
B) self-pollinated crops such as wheat and rice
C) vegetatively propagated crops such as potato
D) perennial fruit trees such as mango
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) self-pollinated crops such as wheat and rice
Why: A pure line is the progeny of a single self-pollinated homozygous plant, so the method works in self-pollinated crops.
Why not the others:
(A) Cross-pollinated crops are heterozygous and cannot be kept as pure lines.
(C) Clonal crops are improved by clonal selection.
(D) Fruit trees are mostly improved by clonal methods.
Key point: Pure-line selection is for self-pollinated crops; clonal selection is for vegetatively propagated ones.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Irrigation and Drainage
questions.sub_topic: What CPE means in irrigation scheduling
questions.question: In the IW/CPE method of scheduling irrigation, CPE stands for ________.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) cumulative pan evaporation
Why: The ratio compares the depth of irrigation water (IW) with the cumulative evaporation from a standard open pan (CPE). The crop is irrigated when CPE reaches the set level.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are made-up expansions.
Key point: IW/CPE ties irrigation to measured evaporation.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Genetics and Plant Breeding
questions.sub_topic: Why meiosis matters in sexual reproduction
questions.question: Why is meiosis essential in sexually reproducing crop plants?
options: A) Because it doubles the chromosome number in every new cell formed
B) Because it produces daughter cells identical to the parent cell
C) Because it halves the chromosome number in gametes
D) Because it occurs only in root tips, where most growth takes place
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Because it halves the chromosome number in gametes
Why: Meiosis forms haploid gametes; when two gametes fuse, the diploid number is restored, so it stays constant from one generation to the next. Crossing over in meiosis also creates new combinations of genes.
Why not the others:
(A) Meiosis halves the number; it does not double it.
(B) Identical daughter cells are the result of mitosis.
(D) Root tips divide by mitosis; meiosis occurs in reproductive organs.
Key point: Meiosis halves; fertilisation restores.

questions.topic: Unit 2 (Livestock Production): Livestock: Scope, Importance and Breeds
questions.sub_topic: Species to which native cattle belong
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

India's native cattle belong to the humped zebu type, *Bos indicus*. They are well suited to hot climates: they have loose skin, many sweat glands and a natural resistance to ticks and several tropical diseases, and they can live on coarse fodder. Breeds are grouped by use. Gir from the Saurashtra region of Gujarat and Red Sindhi are known for milk. Hallikar and Amritmahal of Karnataka are valued for draught power. Tharparkar from the Thar desert and Kankrej from north Gujarat are dual-purpose: the cows give fair amounts of milk and the bullocks work well. Because most native cows give only modest yields, exotic dairy breeds such as Holstein Friesian and Jersey were crossed with them. The crossbred cows give much more milk, but they suffer more in hot weather and need better feed and care. In 1970 the National Dairy Development Board launched Operation Flood. It spread the Anand pattern, in which village milk societies send milk to a district union, and the unions form a state federation that markets the milk and its products. Farmers own the whole chain and receive most of the consumer's rupee. Within three decades India became the world's largest producer of milk. In 2014 the government began the Rashtriya Gokul Mission to conserve and improve indigenous breeds, so that their hardiness is not lost in the rush to cross them with exotic bulls.

Question: According to the passage, India's native cattle belong to:
options: A) *Bos indicus*, the humped zebu type
B) *Bos taurus*, the humpless European type
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) *Bos indicus*, the humped zebu type
Why: The passage says India's native cattle are of the humped zebu type, *Bos indicus*.
Why not the others:
(B) *Bos taurus* covers exotic breeds such as Holstein Friesian and Jersey.
(C) *Bubalus bubalis* is the buffalo, not cattle.
(D) *Capra hircus* is the goat.
Key point: Indian cattle are zebu (*Bos indicus*); European cattle are *Bos taurus*.

questions.topic: Unit 2 (Livestock Production): Livestock: Scope, Importance and Breeds
questions.sub_topic: Dual-purpose breed from the Thar desert
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Question: Which breed does the passage describe as a dual-purpose breed from the Thar desert?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Tharparkar
Why: The passage names Tharparkar from the Thar desert, with Kankrej, as dual-purpose breeds.
Why not the others:
(A) Gir and (C) Red Sindhi are named for milk.
(B) Hallikar is named for draught.
Key point: Tharparkar and Kankrej give both milk and draught power.

questions.topic: Unit 2 (Livestock Production): Livestock: Scope, Importance and Breeds
questions.sub_topic: Tiers of the Anand pattern
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

In 2014 the government began the Rashtriya Gokul Mission to conserve and improve indigenous breeds, so that their hardiness is not lost in the rush to cross them with exotic bulls.

Question: In the Anand pattern described in the passage, the three tiers from bottom to top are:
options: A) district union, village society, national board
B) village society, district union, state federation
C) state federation, district union, village society
D) village society, block office, national federation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) village society, district union, state federation
Why: The passage says village milk societies send milk to a district union, and the unions form a state federation that markets the milk.
Why not the others:
(A) and (C) put the tiers in the wrong order.
(D) A block office and a national federation are not part of the pattern the passage describes.
Key point: The Anand pattern runs village society → district union → state federation.

questions.topic: Unit 2 (Livestock Production): Livestock: Scope, Importance and Breeds
questions.sub_topic: Why crossbred cows need care
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

They are well suited to hot climates: they have loose skin, many sweat glands and a natural resistance to ticks and several tropical diseases, and they can live on coarse fodder. Farmers own the whole chain and receive most of the consumer's rupee. Within three decades India became the world's largest producer of milk. In 2014 the government began the Rashtriya Gokul Mission to conserve and improve indigenous breeds, so that their hardiness is not lost in the rush to cross them with exotic bulls.

Question: Which conclusion about crossbred cows can be drawn from the passage?
options: A) They give less milk than native cows but tolerate heat better.
B) They are preferred because they live on coarse fodder alone.
C) They raise yields, but at the cost of some of the native cow's hardiness.
D) They were introduced after 2014 under the Rashtriya Gokul Mission.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) They raise yields, but at the cost of some of the native cow's hardiness.
Why: The passage says crossbreds give much more milk but suffer more in heat and need better feed and care, which is why native hardiness needs protecting.
Why not the others:
(A) This reverses the passage.
(B) The passage says crossbreds need better feed.
(D) Crossbreeding came before the mission; the mission conserves native breeds.
Key point: Crossbreeding trades hardiness for yield, so native breeds are conserved.

questions.topic: Unit 2 (Livestock Production): Livestock: Scope, Importance and Breeds
questions.sub_topic: Claim not supported by the cattle passage

Question: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the passage?
options: A) Operation Flood was launched by the National Dairy Development Board in 1970.
B) Farmers own the whole chain in the Anand pattern.
C) The Rashtriya Gokul Mission aims to conserve indigenous breeds.
D) Hallikar and Amritmahal are mainly kept for their milk.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Hallikar and Amritmahal are mainly kept for their milk.
Why: The passage says Hallikar and Amritmahal are valued for draught power, not milk.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are all stated in the passage.
Key point: Hallikar and Amritmahal are draught breeds of Karnataka.
